cues.text: Dave Ramsey makes retirement sound simple.
Earn 12%. Inflation takes 4%. Live off 8%.
$40,000 a year takes just $500,000.
Joe and Suzy save $625 a month, age 30 to 70.
The book says: $7.59 million.
What if I'm half wrong? Four million. Six times wrong?
Let's check, against real history.
First: do prices rise 4% a year?
Since 1926, about 2.9%. Since the book, 2.6%.
That one holds up.
Next, the 12%. Up 30, down 10, up 25, up 3. That averages 12%.
But $10,000 grows as if it earned 10.8%.
From 1926 to 2002, the S&P 500 averaged 11.9%, but compounded 10%.
Since 1981, no 30-year stretch compounded 12%. Half right.
Now Joe and Suzy, through all six real 40-year stretches since 1981.
$625 a month became $3.6 to $5.9 million. Never $7.6. Half wrong.
After inflation: $1.2 to $2 million. Closer to six times wrong.
Even a steady 12% makes only $6.1 million.
Then the 8%. Picture a perfect world: 12% and 4%, every year.
$40,000 from $500,000, paid monthly, runs out in year 38.
The most that lasts is 7.52%. $40,000 needs about $532,000.
Now real markets, with real inflation.
Since 1981, 11 of 16 thirty-year S&P retirements kept up.
Back to 1926, just 29 of 71. 35 ran out.
Everyone who retired from 2004 to 2008 ran out or fell behind.
The year you start matters most.
So, half wrong? About that, yes.
Saving still beats not saving, by a mile.
The numbers are just too tidy.
